title: Good teachers don’t cheat
Good teachers don’t cheat
text:
Background
Suppose we have a base policy \(\pi_0(y \mid x)\) and we are interested in learning the policy
\[
\pi^*(y \mid x) \propto \pi_0(y \mid x) \exp\!\big(R(x,y)/\beta\big).
\]
With binary rewards and \(\beta \to 0\), this collapses to \(\pi^*(y \mid x) \propto \pi_0(y \mid x)\,\mathbf{1}_{\{R(x,y) = 1\}}\) i.e., the base policy restricted to correct answers.1
We can characterize RL as an ELBO bound on the partition function \(Z(x)\): \[
\begin{aligned}
Z(x) &= \mathbb{E}_{y \sim \pi_0(\cdot \mid x)} \left[ \exp\!\big(R(x,y)/\beta\big) \right]
\end{aligned}
\]
For any distribution \(q(\cdot \mid x) \ll \pi_0(\cdot \mid x)\) (i.e., \(q(y \mid x) > 0\) implies \(\pi_0(y \mid x) > 0\)), we can rewrite this as an importance-weighted expectation under \(q\):
\[
Z(x) = \mathbb{E}_{y \sim q(\cdot \mid x)} \left[ \frac{\pi_0(y \mid x)}{q(y \mid x)} \exp\!\big(R(x,y)/\beta\big) \right].
\]
By Jensen’s inequality and concavity of \(\log\),
\[
\begin{aligned}
\log Z(x) &\geq \mathbb{E}_{y \sim q(\cdot \mid x)} \left[ R(x,y)/\beta - \log \frac{q(y \mid x)}{\pi_0(y \mid x)} \right] \\
\beta \log Z(x) &\geq \mathbb{E}_{y \sim q(\cdot \mid x)} \left[ R(x,y) \right] - \beta\, \KL{q(\cdot \mid x)}{\pi_0(\cdot \mid x)},
\end{aligned}
\]
where equality holds iff \(\frac{\pi_0(y \mid x)}{q(y \mid x)} \exp(R(x,y)/\beta)\) is constant over all \(y\) with \(q(y \mid x) > 0\); namely, when \(q(y \mid x) = \pi^*(y \mid x)\). It is well known that
\[
\pi^*(y \mid x) = \argmax_q\; \mathbb{E}_{y \sim q(\cdot \mid x)} \left[ R(x,y) \right] - \beta\, \KL{q(\cdot \mid x)}{\pi_0(\cdot \mid x)},
\]
and this is the \(\mathbb{E}_\pi[R] - \beta\KL{\pi}{\pi_0}\) objective that policy gradient methods (GRPO, etc.) typically solve.
As a caveat, we note that some policy gradient methods actually train with \(\beta=0\) for RLVR problems. However, from RL’s Razor we know that on-policy RL methods implicitly bound KL divergence, making this a reasonable assumption.

title: Good teachers don’t cheat
section: Privileged information, and why good teachers don’t cheat
text:
Privileged information, and why good teachers don’t cheat
Now suppose we have privileged information \(z \sim \rho(\cdot \mid x)\) (for example, \(z \in \mathcal{Y}\) is an expert demonstration of a problem \(x\)) that makes it easier to obtain high rewards. In the simplest case \(z = f(x)\) for some deterministic function \(f\) (e.g., a lookup table over stored answers).
Fix \(z \sim \rho(\cdot \mid x)\) and parameterize a distribution \(g(\cdot \mid x, z)\) with \(g(\cdot \mid x, z) \ll \pi_0(\cdot \mid x)\). Applying the ELBO bound from above, we have almost trivially: \[
\begin{aligned}
\beta \log Z(x) &\geq \mathbb{E}_{y \sim g(\cdot \mid x, z)} \left[ R(x,y) \right] - \beta\, \KL{g(\cdot \mid x, z)}{\pi_0(\cdot \mid x)}.
\end{aligned}
\]
That is, for any \(z \sim \rho(\cdot \mid x)\), the optimal \(g(\cdot \mid x, z)\) that achieves the bound is
\[
g(y \mid x, z) = \pi^*(y \mid x),
\]
which does not depend on \(z\)!
The KL term is what makes this work, despite \(\beta\) being possibly vanishingly small. Suppose \(z\) is an expert demonstration containing the final answer, say \(42\). Then \(g(y \mid x, z) = \mathbf{1}_{\{y = 42\}}\) achieves the optimal reward, but it has extremely high KL divergence from \(\pi_0\), and is therefore not feasible to distill into the student. It is difficult to distill a teacher which simply repeats the final answer into the student.

title: Good teachers don’t cheat
section: RL, self-distillation, and Pedagogical RL are all equivalent
text:
RL, self-distillation, and Pedagogical RL are all equivalent
This gives us two ways to optimize the same \(\mathbb{E}_\pi[R] - \beta\KL{\pi}{\pi_0}\) objective:

Start from \(\pi(y \mid x) = \pi_0(y \mid x)\). Sparse rewards, but \(\KL{\pi_0}{\pi_0} = 0\). GRPO and the like.
Start from \(\pi_0(y \mid x, z)\). Dense rewards, but large KL. Pedagogical RL and on-policy-distillation follow this paradigm.

Importantly, KL divergence is significantly easier to optimize than sparse rewards, since rich gradients can be derived from full per-token logits (see this).
The above motivates the following two-stage procedure:

Train the teacher \(g(y \mid x, z)\) to optimize \(\mathbb{E}_g[R] - \beta\KL{g}{\pi_0}\). At optimality, \(g(y \mid x, z)\) loses its dependence on \(z\).
Distill the teacher \(g(y \mid x, z)\) into the student \(\pi(y \mid x)\) via KL minimization, since \(z\) is not available at test time. The direction of the KL is exactly the choice between two distillation methods:

Minimizing \(\KL{\pi(\cdot \mid x)}{g(\cdot \mid x, z)}\) is exactly on-policy distillation.
Minimizing \(\KL{g(\cdot \mid x, z)}{\pi(\cdot \mid x)}\) is equivalent to maximizing \(\mathbb{E}_{y \sim g(\cdot \mid x, z)}[\log \pi(y \mid x)]\), which is standard off-policy SFT, which Pedagogical RL argues is more sample-efficient than on-policy distillation.


So policy gradients, self-distillation, and Pedagogical RL can be interpreted as three different optimization procedures for the same underlying objective \(\mathbb{E}_\pi[R] - \beta\KL{\pi}{\pi_0}\), differing in their use of \(z\) and the direction of KL minimization.

title: Good teachers don’t cheat
text:
Self-distillation woes
The problem with most on-policy distillation techniques is that the teacher \(g(y \mid x, z) = \pi_0(y \mid x, z)\) is never trained to optimize \(\mathbb{E}_g[R] - \beta\KL{g}{\pi_0}\), step 1 is skipped! As a result, the teacher is not guaranteed to lose its dependence on \(z\), and on-policy distillation leaks the privileged information straight into the student. This probably causes the various stability issues observed in on-policy-distillation methods, with student and teacher logits diverging irreconcilably.
This post hints at the direction of some ongoing work; more to come!

title: A critical look at self-distillation for reasoning
A critical look at self-distillation for reasoning
text:
What does self-distillation promise?
Wait; what made self-distillation so appealing to begin with? Let us have a peek at some results and claims made in self-distillation papers.



Motivation for on-policy self-distillation: the model learns by internalizing ground-truth solutions (from page 4 of OPSD)


OPSD claims that having a model internalize ground-truth solutions (via self-distillation) allows it to “teach itself”. This contrasts with the standard reinforcement learning paradigm, which learns by trial and error (e.g., GRPO needs both successful and unsuccessful rollouts to learn).



SDPO vs. GRPO accuracy on LiveCodeBench v6 with Qwen3-8B (Figure 1 of SDPO)


SDPO claims to improve over GRPO performance on LiveCodeBench v6, by leveraging the “model’s ability to retrospectively identify its own mistakes in-context” and dense logit-level feedback to achieve both sample complexity and performance gains.



SDPO takeaway on science reasoning (SciKnowEval) and tool use (ToolAlpaca) (from page 7 of SDPO)


SDPO claims to demonstrate generalization and wall-clock speedups on hard reasoning tasks, training on science reasoning and tool use tasks.



Accuracy of SFT, GRPO, and OPSD on AIME24, AIME25, and HMMT25 across Qwen3 models (Table 2 of OPSD)


On standard math benchmarks, OPSD claims that the use of privileged information yields consistent performance gains over GRPO, by “utilizing its own rationalization ability to grade its weaker self without access to the ground truth.”
This is why self-distillation is appealing: it promises to allow us to use the model’s own internalization of environmental feedback to improve itself, instead of relying on external supervision.

Why might self-distillation work?



The in-context learning assumption behind self-distillation: a demonstration-conditioned model approximates the optimal policy (Section 3.2 of Shenfeld et al.)


To justify self-distillation, Shenfeld et al. hypothesize that self-distillation works because feeding the model with privileged information (e.g., reference solutions) allows it to approximate the optimal policy \[\pi^* = \argmax_\pi \mathbb{E}_{y\sim \pi}[R(y)]-\beta \KL{\pi}{\pi_0}.\]
And indeed! We show in Proposition 3.1 of our paper that if \(\pi_\theta(\cdot|z)=\pi^*(\cdot)\), then self-distillation is equivalent to directly performing gradient ascent on the expected reward. Under this assumption, self-distillation should maximize the same objective as GRPO, just with better sample efficiency afforded by dense logit-level feedback.

This seems to indicate that by and large1, self-distillation gradients are orthogonal or even anti-aligned with the reward maximization gradient. By a Taylor series argument, with small enough steps, following the self-distillation gradient will not improve the expected reward, and may even hurt it.
Wait, so how do you explain the previously reported performance gains?

Overfitting abounds
Note the following excerpt from page 8 of the SDPO paper:

We consider a setting with public and private unit tests, common for code contests and coding platforms like LeetCode, where the public tests are used for evaluation during training and the private tests are used for validation.

In other words, SDPO evaluates on the same LiveCodeBench v6 problems it trains on, doing train-test splitting only across unit tests. Doing proper train-test splitting across problems yields the following curves:



Performance of GRPO and SDPO on LiveCodeBench v6 using Qwen3-8B


We see that although SDPO learns faster than GRPO on the training set (on both seen and unseen unit tests), it overfits to the training problems, and performs worse than GRPO on unseen problems. Moreover, training for longer than the ~80 steps that SDPO uses (marked in red) shows that GRPO beats even SDPO on the training problems given enough time.

We find that although SDPO and GRPO perform similarly on the training domains, SDPO degrades performance on out-of-distribution domains, consistent with the overfitting hypothesis.


Unprivileged information
Recall that OPSD claims that it works by “exploit[ing] the ground-truth solution \(y^*\) directly as privileged information during training, enabling the model to serve as its own teacher”. But a careful reading of OPSD reveals that the OPSD teacher differs from its student in two ways: the teacher sees the reference solution, and the teacher has Qwen3’s thinking mode turned on, while the student has it turned off. Moreover, note that they also report validation performance with thinking mode turned on.
So which one matters? We find that really, it doesn’t matter what \(y^*\) you feed into the model; you can feed a random solution or no solution at all, and OPSD performance is largely unchanged and even improves in some cases.

Turning on teacher thinking improves thinking-off accuracy by 17.3 points on average, while swapping in the reference solution of a different problem changes it by at most 0.4 points. Without teacher thinking, OPSD barely improves over the base model at all.
Looking at the generations, we find that thinking-off students trained with a thinking teacher learn to think anyway, breaking their non-thinking mode, and this is what leads to performance improvements. OPSD’s gains come from leaking thinking-mode behavior into the non-thinking mode, which requires no privileged information at all.

title: A critical look at self-distillation for reasoning
text:
Conclusion
So, does self-distillation improve reasoning? Not in the way it promises to.
Self-distillation was supposed to let a model teach itself, turning privileged information into a dense, sample-efficient learning signal. Instead, we find that its reported gains either don’t generalize, or don’t come from privileged information at all:

SDPO improves on the problems it trains on, at the cost of new problems and other domains
OPSD gains just as much or more when the reference solution is shuffled or removed; what it really transfers is thinking-mode behavior
Both produce gradients that largely point away from reward maximization on held-out problems

We hope that this work encourages algorithmic development of reinforcement learning methods that actually leverage privileged information to yield robust performance gains.
